title: Caching and batch processing: two ways to reduce costs

opening.headline: Learn how to reduce costs by applying prompt caching to requests that send the same first part repeatedly and batch processing to bulk operations that do not require an immediate response.
body: I have a service that sends thousands of tokens of the same system prompt over and over again with every request. Meanwhile, we're also busy sorting out tens of thousands of inquiries every night. In the former case, it is a waste to recalculate the same input each time, and in the latter case, it is a waste to pay a real-time price even though an immediate response is not required.

In this class, we'll explore what prompt caching reuses and under what conditions Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini provide caching. Next, we compare the conditions of the batch API, which reduces the cost by 50%, and provide commentary on cases of diagnosing requests that do not hit the cache and designing nightly bulk classification.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principles and conditions of prompt caching and batch API
Cache hits can be diagnosed based on response usage information.
Depending on the nature of the request, you can choose the appropriate method between caching and batching.

screens.title: The cost of long fixed prompts and nightly bulk jobs
screens.lead: First, read about two situations where money is leaking. I read it thinking about what a waste each of the two situations would be.

visual.alt: Two situation cards, side by side, depicting long repetitive system prompts and nightly bulk sorting tasks.
labels: Situation B: Bulk sorting at night
How to reduce these two wastes

paragraphs: Let's compare the two situations. In situation A, the customer-facing chatbot sends the same system prompt worth thousands of tokens for each request. The questions are different every time, but the front page containing the policy document and directive does not change a single word. The model recalculates this front end from scratch for each request.

Situation B involves sorting through tens of thousands of inquiries every night. The results are only needed for the morning report, so there is no reason to get a response right now. However, you are paying the same price as a real-time request.

The two wastes have different causes. A is a waste of recalculating the same input every time, and B is a waste of paying for an immediate response for something that could have waited. The question we will address in this lesson is how each of these two wastes can be reduced.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: What are the means to reduce costs in repetitive inputs and waitable operations respectively?

screens.outro: First, let's think about whether any of my requests have repetitive input and tasks that can wait.

screens.title: Repeated input and non-real-time operations
screens.lead: Does my service have repetitive inputs and non-real-time operations? When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Where is the text that has the same beginning in each request?
items.answer: Examples include system prompts, tool definitions, lengthy reference documentation, and example packs. This content remains the same even if the user question changes, and often makes up the majority of the service's input tokens. The starting point for caching is finding repeated leading parts.

items.prompt: What tasks don’t require results right now?
items.answer: This involves running evaluations, bulk sorting, creating embeds, and reviewing content, and then writing the results all at once. For tasks that don't involve users waiting in front of a screen, you can lower costs at the expense of responsiveness. This is the starting point for batch processing.

It is possible. If you are running a large volume of requests overnight and all requests start with the same sorting instructions, you can use both methods together. However, in batch, requests are processed asynchronously and concurrently, so cache hits are not guaranteed and are served on a best-effort basis.

screens.outro: First, let's take a step-by-step look at the principles of caching.

screens.title: Prompt caching: Do not recalculate prefixes
screens.lead: The following steps demonstrate how prompt caching works for first and subsequent requests. Select the right arrow to go through the steps one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration of a two-line token where a prefix is saved in the first request and the same prefix is reused in the second request.

steps.title: Processing input creates an intermediate state.
steps.body: As the model processes input tokens, it creates intermediate computation results called key-value states so that it can reference previous tokens. Creating this state costs as much computation as the input token. The longer the input, the greater the computation time and cost.

steps.title: Preserve the state of the prefix
steps.body: Prompt caching stores the state of the part before the prompt, or prefix. If a subsequent request comes with the same prefix, the saved state is reused. What is stored is not the token itself, but rather the computed key-value state.

steps.title: Compute only new inputs
steps.body: Reused sections are not recalculated, making them faster and reducing input costs. You only need to process the newly added question part. OpenAI explains that discounted rates of up to 95% apply for reused input tokens.

steps.title: The entire prefix must match
steps.body: A cache is only reused if the prefixes match from beginning to end. If the content changes somewhere in the middle, it will not be reused after that. Claude's hash is calculated by accumulating the content up to the breakpoint, so even if just one letter at the beginning is changed, the entire following part becomes a different prefix.

steps.title: Fixed content at the front, changing content at the back.
steps.body: So when designing prompts, put directives, policy documents, and tool definitions that don't change first, and put things that change, like visuals or user questions, at the end. Claude's cache is prefixed in the following order: tool, system, message, and when the top is changed, the bottom becomes invalid as well.

steps.title: A cache has a lifetime and a minimum length.
steps.body: Cache only lasts for a certain amount of time. Claude's default lifetime is 5 minutes, and is renewed at no additional cost each time the cache is used. Also, if the prefix is ​​shorter than the minimum token length determined by the model, it will not be cached and no error will be generated.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the principle, let's compare side by side under what conditions the three providers provide caching.

screens.title: View the caching conditions of the three companies side by side
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini turn on caching, minimum length, and see the effect.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Prompt caching is turned on by default on supported models. In implicit mode, OpenAI determines the location of cache breakpoints, while in explicit mode, developers can set breakpoints themselves.

**Minimum Length and Cost**: The minimum length that can be cached is 1,024 tokens in GPT-5.6 and later, and reused input tokens are discounted by up to 95%. At the default 30-minute lifetime for GPT-5.6 and later models, cache writes are 1.25x the typical input and reads are mostly 0.1x.

**Check**: View your cache hit rate in the Prompt Caching Dashboard, and use diagnostic tools to find out why you're missing a hit.

tabs.label: Claude: Automatic caching
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Place `cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"}` as a line at the top of the request. The system prefixes the last cacheable block, and automatically moves the breakpoint forward as the conversation becomes longer. Best suited for conversations with multiple turns.

**Life and Cost**: The default life is 5 minutes and renews at no additional cost each time you use it. Lifetime is calculated from the time the request is initiated, so it also includes the time to generate the response. A one-hour lifetime can be specified as twice the base input price. In most models, cache writes cost 25% more than the base input, and reads cost 10% of the base input.

tabs.label: Claude: Explicit breakpoints
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: If you add `"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}` to an individual content block, such as a system block, the contents up to that block will be cached. Use this when you want to decide in detail how much to cache.

**Caution**: Even if you mark just one breakpoint, the system will look backwards and check the longest prefix written by the previous request, but the range it will go back and check at a time is 20 blocks. The only place we write cache is at breakpoints, so we need to mark the last block that doesn't change. Breakpoints themselves do not add any cost.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Implicit caching is turned on by default on Gemini 2.5 and later models, so there is nothing to configure. Savings are automatically reflected when a request hits the cache.

**Minimum Length**: Each model has a set minimum input token. For example, the Gemini 2.5 Flash and 2.5 Pro cost 2,048 tokens, and many of the newer models cost 4,096 tokens.

**How ​​to increase your hit rate**: Place large, common content at the beginning of the prompt, and send requests with similar prefixes within a short period of time.

screens.outro: Now that we've compared caching conditions, let's now compare batch APIs for awaitable operations.

screens.title: Batch API: Cheap if you can wait
screens.lead: Switch between the two states below to compare the differences in price, time, and limits between processing the same job in real time and in batches.

visual.alt: Batch processing flow diagram where requests are collected, submitted to a file, and results received later.

states.label: Real-time request
states.body:
Send them one by one and receive a response right away. Pricing is standard, and responses are usually returned within seconds. Interactive services where the user waits in front of the screen require this approach.

However, if you send tens of thousands of calls in a row, you may hit your call limit, and you'll pay the same price for tasks that don't require an immediate response.

states.label: batch processing
states.body:
Collect requests, submit them all at once, and receive results later. All three providers charge 50% of the standard price.

**Claude Message Batches**: A batch can be up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB. Most will be completed within an hour, and will expire within 24 hours if not completed.

**OpenAI Batch API**: Submit one request per line in the `.jsonl` file. It completes within 24 hours and has separate limits that are much higher than real-time calls.

**Gemini Batch**: 50% of standard cost with target turnaround time of 24 hours. Send it as an inline request or input file.

Suitable tasks include running assessments, bulk sorting, generating embeds, and reviewing content.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the conditions for both methods, let us explain an example of diagnosing a request that does not hit the cache.

screens.title: Case Study: Reading Requests That Don't Hit the Cache
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of diagnosing requests whose cost does not decrease even when the cache is turned on, using the usage information in the response. Select the right arrow to follow the steps.

steps.title: request structure
steps.body: The first line of system is `Current time: 2026-10-22 09:14`, followed by a policy document with thousands of tokens, and the last block is `cache_control`. This is followed by user questions.

steps.title: Symptom: Can only write but cannot read
steps.body: The response has a usage of `{"cache_creation_input_tokens": 5200, "cache_read_input_tokens": 0}` and this is repeated for each request. The 5,200 tokens keep being written again and cannot be read even once. Cache is turned on but has no effect.

steps.title: Step 1: Find the cause
steps.body: The time at the beginning is different for each request, so the entire prefix does not match. If the previous one is changed, it will not be reused, no matter how similar the policy document behind it may be. A breakpoint marks a write, and a read only occurs if a previous request has already written the same prefix.

steps.title: Step 2: Gather your pinned content in front of you
steps.body: Move the visual line to the end of the user message, behind the fixed section, and bring the policy document to the front. `cache_control` is placed at the end of the last block that does not change. Now, even if the time changes, the prefix remains the same.

steps.title: Step 3: Check the minimum length
steps.body: Ensure that the prefix exceeds the model's minimum cache length. If both fields return 0, no caching has occurred at all, and a common cause is that the length is less than the minimum. There is no error at this time, so you can tell by looking at the usage field directly.

steps.title: Step 4: Check the effect with a second request
steps.body: After fixing it, send a second request to the same prefix to see if the usage changes to something like `{"input_tokens": 40, "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0, "cache_read_input_tokens": 5200}`. This means that 5,200 tokens were reused from the cache and the new count was 40 tokens. Gemini confirms the same with `usage.total_cached_tokens`.

screens.outro: Now that we have verified the caching diagnostics, let's look at an example of a nightly bulk job with appropriate placement.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Nighttime Bulk Sorting
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the process of designing a task that sorts through tens of thousands of inquiries each night. Select the right arrow to follow the steps.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing real-time processing cost bars and batch processing cost bars for the same job.

steps.title: work
steps.body: We triage tens of thousands of inquiries every night. Results are first written in the morning report, so it is sufficient to finish overnight.

steps.title: Step 1: Gather requests
steps.body: Each inquiry is made into one request and collected into a jsonl file or batch request bundle. Claude can accommodate up to 100,000 requests, or 256MB, in a single batch, so tens of thousands of requests can be submitted in a single batch.

steps.title: Step 2: Look at the time required and adjust the submission time
steps.body: Placements are based on completion within 24 hours. Most will finish much earlier, but since completion times cannot be guaranteed, submit well in advance of the morning report. Requests not processed within 24 hours will expire and you will not be charged for expired requests.

steps.title: Step 3: If your pinning instructions are long, consider caching as well
steps.body: Caching can also be used if each request is prefixed with the same classification instructions. Discounts from both methods stack. However, batch requests are processed asynchronously and concurrently, so it is a best effort cache hit and not guaranteed. The probability of a hit is increased by inserting the same `cache_control` block into all requests and ensuring that requests flow uninterruptedly.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Anything that can wait can be done in batches at half the price, and if there's a repeating front end, add caching. Only use caching for interactive requests that require an immediate response. The nature of the request determines the means.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the two cases, I will conclude by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Use caching for repetitive input and batching for waitable operations. Caching is most effective when the same request continues to come in, while batching is effective for bulk operations that do not require an immediate response.

To hit the cache, place static content before the prompt and changing content after it. The effectiveness is confirmed by the Cache Write and Read fields in the response usage. If both fields are 0, no caching has occurred; a common cause is not meeting the minimum length.

The two tools can be used together. However, in batches, cache hits are provided on a best-effort basis, so the cost calculation is not entirely dependent on hits, and usage determines the actual effect. Classifying which category your request falls into is the first step to reducing costs.

glossary.def: This feature reduces cost and delay by reusing calculation results from the same prompt prefix.
This is an unchanging section that continues from the beginning of the prompt. The cache is only reused if the entire prefix matches.
An API that lowers costs by 50% instead of gathering requests and processing them asynchronously.
This is a task that does not require an immediate response, so you can receive results later.

misconceptions.myth: Caching stores previous responses and returns the same response.
misconceptions.fact: What is cached is the computational state of the input prefix. Since the output is generated anew each time, the answer to the same question may vary.

misconceptions.myth: Even if you change the middle of the prefix, the cache is used as is.
misconceptions.fact: To be reused, the entire prefix must match, and will not be reused beyond the point where it was changed. Anything that changes should be left behind.
Although most are completed quickly, completion time should be up to 24 hours. It is not used for tasks that require an immediate response.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Caching is used for repetitive input, and batching is used for tasks that can wait.
You need to place the fixed content before the prompt to hit the cache.
Batch gives up immediate response in exchange for a 50% cost reduction.
The effect is confirmed by the cache write and read fields of the response usage.
